summary: This informational document gives the problem statement, use cases and framework for managing telephone numbers on the Internet. Phone numbers no longer simply route calls but also serve as identifiers for many services. The document describes the needs as telephony moves to the Internet.

eli5.summary: A phone number used to be just a way to ring a phone. Now it also says who you are online. This explains how to handle that.

questions: what is the modern working group
how are telephone numbers managed on the internet
what is a registrar for telephone numbers
what is the difference between administrative and service data
subtitle: Why Internet services need new ways to hand out, manage and look up telephone numbers, and the framework proposed.

tldr.problem: Telephone numbers now act as identifiers for Internet services, but the tools for allocating and managing them were built for the geographic, carrier-centred telephone network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the actors (such as Registry, Registrar and Communication Service Provider), two kinds of data (administrative and service) and three Internet-based mechanisms: acquisition, management and retrieval.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement and framework for the IETF MODERN Working Group, not a protocol: it expects existing protocols to be reused and new information models to be the main work.

facts.label: Example block sizes
facts.value: 10,000 TNs to a CSP, 100 to a PBX

today: RFC 8396 is an Informational document published in July 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it states the problem and framework rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: The Problem with Telephone Numbers on the Internet
sections.content:
Internet telephony first used telephone numbers (TNs) in ways similar to the Public Switched Telephone Network. ENUM (RFC 6116) built a DNS-based way to turn TNs into URIs for protocols such as SIP. It was meant to be a global hierarchy, but in practice it was deployed piecemeal and is mostly an internal network function. The single root, e164.arpa, proved politically and practically hard, according to the RFC.

Meanwhile, enterprises, over-the-top VoIP providers and text messaging services have become heavy users of numbers. Internet portals let people allocate numbers on the fly or assign several alias numbers to one line. Number portability, which lets a user keep a TN when changing provider, exists in many countries, but processes rooted in PSTN technology made porting slow and problem-prone.

Numbers are also tied to geography in the PSTN, while IP network topology is not. The RFC says adapting TNs to the Internet needs more security, richer datasets and more complex query and response capabilities than earlier efforts provided. It sets out to create a common understanding of the problem for the MODERN Working Group, and says solutions must be flexible about differing national policies.
sections.eli5: Phone numbers used to be handed out by the phone company, tied to a place. Now apps and websites use them too, and the old way is slow and does not fit.

sections.title: Actors and Data Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines these actors. A Numbering Authority is a regulatory body that sets policy on which TNs may be allocated. A Registry administers allocation under that policy. A Registrar distributes numbers from a Registry and deals with the assignees. A Communication Service Provider (CSP) provides service identified by TNs, and may be a traditional carrier, an enterprise or a provider with no PSTN presence. Others are the Credential Authority, the Service Enabler, the User and the Government Entity. One entity can play several roles.

Numbers flow down a chain. An assignee gets a TN directly from a Registrar, and a delegate gets one from an assignee or another delegate. The RFC's example has a Registry issuing blocks of 10,000 TNs to a CSP acting as Registrar, which gives 100 to an enterprise PBX, which gives 1 to a User.

There are two data types. Administrative data covers TN status and contacts, and is not needed in real time. Service data covers addressing and features, such as a SIP URI, and must be available in real time to complete calls. Each can be public, semi-restricted or restricted. The RFC compares this with DNS, where registries and registrars manage names and WHOIS gives administrative data. It also allows distributed data stores and distributed registries.
sections.eli5: There is a rule-maker, a keeper of the big list, shops that hand out numbers, and the people who finally use them. Some facts are for everyone, some for a few, and some only for very special visitors.

sections.title: The Three-Mechanism Framework
sections.content:
The framework requires three Internet-based mechanisms. Acquisition is for acquiring TNs, including enrollment, either number by number or as inventory blocks. Management is for associating data with TNs, for example choosing a CSP to serve a number. Retrieval is for learning information about TNs, usually by asking a CSP for real-time service data, or a Registry for other information.

The RFC expects these to reuse existing protocols for sharing structured data, naming DRINKS (RFC 6461), WEIRDS (RFC 7482) and the TeRI framework. It says new protocol development is unlikely to be required, and that new information models for the data will be a major focus. The mechanisms are meant to fit many future number policies, whether number administration is centralized or not.
sections.eli5: There are three jobs: getting a number, filling in the details about it, and looking it up. The paper says to reuse the tools that already exist for them.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
For acquisition, a CSP can request blocks from a Registrar after an out-of-band business arrangement. The Registrar must authenticate and authorize it, and the Registry records the assignment and removes the numbers from the available pool. The Registry also supplies material that a Credential Authority needs to issue credentials such as STIR certificates (RFC 8226). A User can also get a TN from a CSP when signing up for service, and then becomes its delegate, or directly from a Registrar, as freephone buyers do today.

Management covers administrative data at a Registrar or CSP and service data such as a SIP URI. Low-level changes, like a device getting a new IP address, would use existing protocols such as SIP REGISTER. When a User switches CSP and keeps the number, the old credentials are revoked and new ones issued. On termination, the CSP undoes delegations, removes service data, and the TN goes from assigned to unassigned and would likely enter an aging process.

Retrieval depends on the data category. Public data can be posted on websites or an API. Semi-restricted data, such as a CSP's contact point for troubleshooting or service data in a closed environment, requires the requester to be identified. Restricted data may be reached by a Government Entity, which is authenticated and authorized under the Numbering Authority's policy.
sections.eli5: You can get a number from a shop or from your phone company. You can change who looks after it, and you can hand it back. Looking up details is allowed for different people depending on how private the detail is.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Service data could leak resource locations and even lower-layer network addresses, in rare cases of end-user devices. Administrative data identifies who is behind numbers and in some layers could include personally identifiable information (PII), such as real names and postal addresses. The RFC says the exact nature of administrative data is not defined, so it is hard to say how much PII these services will hold.

If an attacker compromised a Registrar service, PII about end users could leak, so these systems are attractive targets and need hardening. The RFC also notes that in many jurisdictions government agencies have a legal right to access data kept by CSPs, though the administrative data in this framework could be richer.
sections.eli5: The lists contain names and addresses, so they must be locked up well. Some officials are allowed to look, and the paper says out loud that this happens.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Each of the three interfaces needs mutual authentication, integrity protection and confidentiality. For acquisition, a Registry will want to authenticate the requester, and integrity protects against attackers blocking acquisitions or commandeering resources. For management, missing authentication and authorization could let an attacker disrupt data, deny service, enable impersonation or break billing. For retrieval, a CSP wants to know it is reaching the proper authority, that the response was not tampered with, and usually that eavesdroppers cannot see which number it asked about. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Every conversation about numbers needs three things: knowing who you are talking to, making sure nobody changes the message, and keeping it secret from onlookers.

items.title: Acquisition
items.text: Request TNs from a Registrar, CSP or similar actor, one by one or as blocks.

items.title: Management
items.text: Associate administrative and service data with TNs.

items.title: Retrieval
items.text: Learn information about TNs, subject to public, semi-restricted or restricted access.
